facts.text: On this date in 2001, lower Manhattan lost 1.2 million jobs within weeks — yet New York's population reached a record high by 2008, driven partly by a surge in immigration that outpaced the exodus.

On September 11, 1973, Pinochet's coup overthrew Chile's elected government. The presidential palace was bombed by the country's own air force — the first time a Latin American military attacked its own capital from the air.
Mongolia has a lower population density than any other sovereign nation: roughly 2 people per square kilometer, meaning the entire country holds fewer residents than the city of Cologne.
More people live within a 4,000 km radius centered on Bangladesh than in any other circle of equal size on Earth — a region containing over 3.5 billion people across South and Southeast Asia.
Canada is so vast that its coastline — at 202,080 km — is longer than the next four longest coastlines combined, yet over 80% of Canadians live within 150 km of the US border.
On this date in 2001, U.S. markets never opened. When they finally did on Sept 17, the Dow shed 684 points — its largest single-day point drop in history at the time.
On Sept 11, 1789, Alexander Hamilton was appointed the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, laying the foundation for a federal financial system built on assumed debt and central credit.
The NYSE was once regulated by a 1792 agreement signed under a buttonwood tree. The Buttonwood Agreement set fixed commissions and gave its 24 signatories a legal cartel over American securities.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway originally made textiles. He later called buying it the worst investment of his life — estimating the opportunity cost at over $200 billion.
Japan's stock market peaked on December 29, 1989, at 38,957. It took until 2024 — 35 years — to close above that level again.

On this day in 1985, the ICE spacecraft became the first to fly through a comet's tail — Giacobini-Zinner's — sampling plasma that crackled with electromagnetic turbulence never directly measured before.
On September 11, 1877, Charles Henry Melville was born; his later work on yellow fever vaccines saved more lives than any single medical intervention of the early 20th century.
A teaspoon of neutron star material weighs roughly a billion tons on Earth — the same mass as Mount Everest compressed into a space smaller than a sugar cube.
Your body replaces the lining of your small intestine every two to four days, making it one of the fastest-renewing tissues you have — faster even than your skin.
Light takes eight minutes to reach Earth from the Sun, but the photon's energy spent roughly 100,000 years bouncing through the solar interior before it ever reached the surface.
On this day in 1609, Henry Hudson sailed into the harbor that would bear his name — 140 years before the United States existed.
On this day in 2001, the Twin Towers fell. They had stood for just 28 years — shorter than the construction of Cologne Cathedral, which took 632.
The fax machine was patented in 1843, before the American Civil War. Abraham Lincoln could theoretically have sent a fax.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Europe's oldest university predates what we call 'ancient' Mesoamerica.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was separated from the pyramids by more years than from us.
Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and gone. Linguists consider it untranslatable — the word carries the grief and pleasure of absence simultaneously.
Apricity: the warmth of winter sun on your skin. English had this word in 1623, then quietly lost it.
Mamihlapinatapai (Yaghan): the wordless look shared by two people who both want something but neither will initiate. One word does what a novel chapter might.
On this day in 2001, the word 'ground zero' shifted meaning forever — originally military slang for a nuclear blast's epicenter, it became synonymous with a single site in lower Manhattan.
Vellichor is a neologism coined in 2013 by The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows: the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. New words, not just old ones, can achieve instant poetry.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal, triggering a 40% drop in bitcoin within two weeks — the same assets recovered fully within 60 days.
On Sept 11, 2012, Silk Road processed its one-millionth transaction, entirely in bitcoin, on a darknet market the FBI had been monitoring for over a year without being able to seize funds.
Bitcoin's timelock opcode, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, sat unused in the codebase for three years before being activated in BIP 65 — Satoshi had designed it in but never documented why.
The Ethereum genesis block contains a hidden message in its extra data field: a Times headline about bank bailouts — deliberately mirroring Satoshi's own embedded message in Bitcoin's block 0.
Miner Extractable Value (MEV) on Ethereum exceeded $1.3 billion extracted in a single year, most of it invisible to retail users — a structural tax baked into how public mempools work.
On this date in 2001, the 9/11 attacks prompted DARPA to fast-track autonomous systems research — directly funding programs that became foundational to modern drone AI and battlefield perception.
On this date in 2009, Google filed a patent for a neural network-based autocomplete system, years before 'deep learning' entered common use outside academia.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — nearly every known protein on Earth — in roughly 12 months of compute that would have taken classical methods longer than the age of the universe.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed around 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity, roughly equivalent to powering 4,600 average US homes for an entire year.

The first known chess-playing machine that used genuine computation, El Ajedrecista (1912), could solve king-and-rook vs. king endgames autonomously — 45 years before Shannon formalized machine chess strategy.
